Zhejiang province’s rural work leadership group, organization department, development and reform commission, and agriculture and rural affairs bureau jointly issued the "Plan for Supporting and Promoting Relatively Weak Towns and Villages". Title: Adviser to Takaichi's policy circle says weak yen is good for economy

Summary: 
Takuji Aida, chief Japan economist at Credit Agricole and adviser to Sanae Takaichi's policy circle, stated in a Reuters interview that the current weakness of the yen benefits Japan's economy. Takaichi's economic platform reflects the reflationist principles of her policy circle, which advocates proactive government spending to revitalize the economy.

The article argues that while artificial general intelligence (AGI) could theoretically boost global GDP growth to 20‑30 % per year, the resulting boom would largely benefit a small elite and leave tens of millions of workers displaced. The article concludes that while AI may create wealth, it is unclear how that wealth will be distributed.

Title: Mizzou economists: 2025 farm income boosted by high cattle prices and one-time payments

Summary: 
The University of Missouri Food and Agricultural Policy Research Institute (FAPRI) reports that U.S. net farm income is projected to rise sharply to $177 billion in 2025, up from $128 billion in 2024, largely due to record cattle prices and one‑time government payments.  However, the report warns that crop price declines and the expected reduction in future government support could lead to a $31 billion drop in farm income in 2026.  "Despite strong income this year, much of the gain is temporary," said Pat Westhoff, director of FAPRI, noting that "as emergency payments dry up and crop prices remain weak, we project a $31 billion decline in farm income next year."  Key crop price projections include a 2025‑26 marketing‑year corn price of $4.05 per bushel, a soybean price of $10.16 per bushel, and cotton at 66.5 cents per pound; wheat, rice, sorghum and barley remain weak.  Cattle prices are projected to hit new records, with tight supplies and strong domestic demand pushing prices higher in 2026 before increased production moderates them.  Dairy production is expected to rise, but higher supply will weigh on cheese and butter prices, with exports helping to offset the pressure.  Food‑price inflation is projected to rebound to 2.9 % in 2025, driven largely by beef prices, which are expected to rise by more than 10 %.  Food‑at‑home inflation should moderate in 2026, though restaurant costs are likely to continue rising.  Westhoff emphasized that these forecasts are conditional on current policies and market expectations and serve as a benchmark for evaluating future economic shifts, weather events and policy changes.

Title: Beyond the Hype: Technologies That Will Outlive the AI Bubble

Summary: 
The article examines the current 'AI bubble,' a period of inflated expectations and investment in artificial intelligence, drawing parallels to past tech bubbles like the dot-com and blockchain booms. It argues that while the promise of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) has driven massive funding—especially after OpenAI's 2019 shift to a capped-profit model—the inevitable correction will come when AGI fails to materialize or returns don't justify costs. However, the article emphasizes that not all AI-related technologies will collapse; enduring, high-utility technologies will survive and thrive regardless of hype cycles. These include semiconductors (TSMC, NVIDIA, Intel, AMD, Samsung, ASML), cloud computing (AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Alibaba Cloud), quantum computing (IBM, Google, IonQ), cybersecurity (projected to reach $400+ billion by 2030), open-source software (Linux, Kubernetes, PostgreSQL, Python, TensorFlow), data engineering (PostgreSQL, Apache Kafka, Snowflake, Spark, Redis), low-level programming languages (C, C++, Rust), robotics (Amazon, da Vinci, Tesla Gigafactories), the Internet of Things (over 30 billion devices by 2025), network infrastructure (5G, future generations), clean energy technologies (solar, wind, battery storage), DevOps and Platform Engineering, privacy-preserving technologies (differential privacy, zero-knowledge proofs, end-to-end encryption), and digital identity solutions (WebAuthn, biometrics). The article warns against companies relying solely on 'AI' branding without real innovation or business models, and stresses that historical patterns show bubbles eliminate weak ventures while strengthening foundational, problem-solving technologies. The key takeaway: focus on enduring utility, not hype.

These include semiconductors (TSMC, NVIDIA, Intel, AMD, Samsung, ASML), cloud computing (AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Alibaba Cloud), quantum computing (IBM, Google, IonQ), cybersecurity (projected to reach $400+ billion by 2030), open-source software (Linux, Kubernetes, PostgreSQL, Python, TensorFlow), data engineering (PostgreSQL, Apache Kafka, Snowflake, Spark, Redis), low-level programming languages (C, C++, Rust), robotics (Amazon, da Vinci, Tesla Gigafactories), the Internet of Things (over 30 billion devices by 2025), network infrastructure (5G, future generations), clean energy technologies (solar, wind, battery storage), DevOps and Platform Engineering, privacy-preserving technologies (differential privacy, zero-knowledge proofs, end-to-end encryption), and digital identity solutions (WebAuthn, biometrics). The article warns against companies relying solely on 'AI' branding without real innovation or business models, and stresses that historical patterns show bubbles eliminate weak ventures while strengthening foundational, problem-solving technologies. The key takeaway: focus on enduring utility, not hype.

articles.title: Weak Italian GDP and U.S. Tariffs Drive Rise in Corporate Non-Performing Loans, Abi-Cerved Outlook Warns
articles.summary: According to the Abi-Cerved 2025-27 outlook, Italy's weak GDP growth and U.S. tariff policies are driving an increase in corporate non-performing loans, with default rates rising from 2.6% in 2024 to 2.9% in 2025 and expected to reach 3.0% in 2026. Despite this uptick, the report states these rates will remain 'significantly lower' than those seen during previous crises. By 2027, the default rate is projected to decline to 2.9%, matching the 2019 level and far below the 7.5% peak recorded in 2012. The increase in deteriorated credits will affect all geographical regions and economic sectors, with the most pronounced rise occurring in industry, construction, and agriculture.

articles.title: Here's why the ASX 200 could keep climbing higher in 2025
articles.summary: On Wednesday, September 10 2025, the S&P/ASX 200 Index climbed 0.31% to 8,830.40 points, marking a rebound after a weak week. Monday the index fell 0.24% to 8,849.60 points amid weakness in energy and financial sectors and pressure on Woolworths and Coles after a Federal Court ruling. Tuesday it dipped 0.52% to 8,803.5 points due to declines in energy, banking and healthcare, and ANZ's announcement of a large job‑cut initiative, while OPEC+ increased oil production. The rebound on Wednesday was led by the banking sector, with the big four banks gaining 1.47% to 1.70% following cost‑cutting announcements and renewed investor confidence. Macquarie strategist Matthew Brooks told The Australian that conservative company guidance has set a low bar for FY26, creating an ideal condition for future earnings upgrades. He added, 'Conservative guides have set a low bar for FY26. Coupled with the RBA rate cuts and an already improving domestic economy, this could allow for earnings upgrades over FY26,' and 'We could even start to see some more positive outlook comments in AGM season.' The Reserve Bank of Australia has already delivered three rate cuts; lower borrowing costs are expected to boost consumer spending, housing demand and sectors such as consumer staples, retail and real estate. For example, REA Group could benefit from increased property activity and JB Hi‑Fi from higher consumer discretionary spending. With economic growth set to accelerate and conservative guidance, the remainder of 2025 could see ASX 200 growth stronger than originally expected.
